newsitem.title: USA: Air unions demand action against unruly passengers.
newsitem.headline: Air unions demand action against unruly passengers.

text.p: Unruly, often intoxicated passengers are causing dangerous in-flight disturbances and the problem will likely worsen as planes and airports become more crowded, pilots and flight attendants said on Wednesday.
The cockpit and cabin crews called on unions, companies, law enforcement agencies and the Federal Aviation Administration to join together to take tough action.

They told a conference on Disruptive Airline Passengers that incidents included passengers assaulting pilots, trying to break into a cockpit, punching flight attendants and, in one extreme case, a passenger defecating on a food trolley.
In some cases, in-flight handcuffs were used and abusive passengers were arrested when the plane landed.

Randolph Babbitt, president of the Air Line Pilots Association, sponsor of the conference, said the incidents were not only a threat to crew but "a very, very real and serious risk to our passengers."

He said cases of disruptive behaviour would likely increase in the coming years as passenger traffic doubled, planes became more crowded and passengers were forced to spend many hours in airports for lengthier security checks.
"We want to create an awareness among airline travelers that disruptive behaviour is unsafe, and it is also a federal offence that can get you some serious jail time," he said.
In many cases, he said, airlines were reluctant to prosecute passengers, worrying about the impact on marketing and public relations.

However, Kathy Lord-Jones, safety coordinator of the Association of Professional Flight Attendants, a union at American Airlines, said this had changed. She said the carrier's policy now was to press police to file criminal charges and to support crewmembers if they wanted to file civil charges.

She said she wanted the public to become better informed about the consequences of disruptive behaviour. "Whether it be by way of the media or a trip to the local police station in handcuffs, our message, industry-wide, needs to be conveyed, poor behaviour will not be tolerated on any aircraft."

A George Washington University specialist in psychiatry and political psychology told the conference alcohol was often the underlying cause of disruptive actions. Jerrold Post said crowded airports and planes created stress and alcohol triggered extreme reactions in some people.
He said cited three traits among disruptive passengers:

-- Entitlement and a sense of superiority. This was the case of a Saudi princess who scratched an attendant when told to buckle her seat belt. Post paraphrased her as saying "I have never been told by anyone to do anything."

-- Authority. An important businessman with authority in his office may resent authority in others, and alcohol can make this feeling rise when a flight attendant tells him to turn off his laptop computer or hang up the airphone.
-- "Fear of flying," or loss of control. In some cases alcohol may act as a tranquilliser to reduce this fear, but too much can cause disruptive behaviour.
Post also said cigarette deprivation on non-smoking flights could trigger disruptive behaviour.
